text: Embellishment to a city is the valor of its citizens; to a person, comeliness; to a soul, wisdom; to a deed, virtue; to discourse, truth. But the opposite to these is lack of embellishment. Now a man, woman, discourse, work, city, deed, if deserving of praise must be honored with praise, but if undeserving must be censured. For it is alike aberration and stultification to censure the commendable and commend the censurable.

It is the duty of the same individual both to proclaim justice wholly, and to declaim against injustice holily, to confute the detractors of Helen, a woman concerning whom there has been uniform and universal praise of poets and the celebration of her name has been the commemoration of her fame. But I desire by rational calculation to free the lady’s reputation, by disclosing her detractors as prevaricators, and by revealing the truth to put an end to error.

That in nature and nurture the lady was the fairest flower of men and women is not unknown, not even to the few, for her maternity was of Leda, her paternity immortal by generation, but mortal by reputation, Tyndareus and Zeus, of whom the one was reputed in the being, the other was asserted in the affirming; the former, the greatest of humanity, the latter, the lordliest of divinity.

Of such origin she was endowed with godlike beauty, expressed not suppressed, which inspired in many men many mad moods of love, and she, one lovely person, assembled many personalities of proud ambition, of whom some possessed opulent riches, others the fair fame of ancient ancestry; others the vigor of native strength, others the power of acquired wisdom; and all came because of amorous contention and ambitious pretention.

Who he was, however, who won Helen and attained his heart’s desire, and why, and how, I will not say, since to give information to the informed conduces to confirmation but conveys no delectation. Passing over in my present discourse the time now past, I will proceed to the beginning of my intended discussion and will predicate the causes by reason of which it was natural that Helen went to Troy.

For either by the disposition of fortune and the ratification of the gods and the determination of necessity she did what she did, or by violence confounded, or by persuasion dumbfounded or to Love surrendered. If, however, it was against her will, the culpable should not be exculpated. For it is impossible to forestall divine disposals by human proposals. It is a law of nature that the stronger is not subordinated to the weaker but the weaker is subjugated and dominated by the stronger; the stronger is the leader while the weaker is the entreater. Divinity surpasses humanity in might, in sight, and in all else. Therefore, if on fortune and the deity we must visit condemnation, the infamy of Helen should find no confirmation.

But if by violence she was defeated and unlawfully she was treated and to her injustice was meted, clearly her violator as a terrifier was importunate, while she, translated and violated, was unfortunate. Therefore, the barbarian who verbally, legally, actually attempted the barbarous attempt, should meet with verbal accusation, legal reprobation and actual condemnation. For Helen who was violated and from her fatherland separated and from her friends segregated should justly meet with commiseration rather than with defamation. For he was the victor and she was the victim. It is just therefore to sympathize with the latter and anathematize the former.

But if it was through λόγος’s reception and the soul’s deception it is not difficult to defend the situation and forefend the accusation, thus. Λόγος is a powerful potentate, who with frailest, feeblest frame works wonders. For it can put an end to fear and make vexation vanish; it can inspire exultation and increase compassion.

I will show how this is so. For I must indicate this to my hearers for them to predicate. All poetry I ordain and proclaim to be composition in meter; the listeners of which are affected by passionate trepidation and compassionate perturbation and likewise tearful lamentation, since through discourse the soul suffers, as if its own, the felicity and infelicity of property and person of others.

Come let us turn to another consideration. Inspired incantations are provocative of charm and revocative of harm. For the power of song in association with the belief of the soul captures and enraptures and translates the soul with witchery. For there have been discovered arts twain of witchery and sorcery, which are consternation to the heart and perturbation to art.

sections.title: *Encomium of Helen* 11–14
sections.note: Van Hook's translation leaves out §§11–14 and 16–18. LeetLit has translated them from the Greek text of F. Blass (Teubner). The Greek of §12 is damaged; the translation follows its generally accepted sense.

text: How many men have persuaded, and still persuade, how many others about how many things, by shaping a false speech! If everyone had memory of everything past, understanding of everything present and foreknowledge of everything to come, speech would not have the same power to deceive. But as it is, it is not easy to remember the past, nor to examine the present, nor to divine the future; so that on most matters most people take opinion as the adviser of their soul. And opinion, being slippery and insecure, casts those who rely on it into slippery and insecure fortunes.

What reason, then, prevents us from concluding that Helen too came under the influence of speech, just as unwillingly as if she had been seized by the force of the violent? For persuasion, though it does not have the look of necessity, has the same power. Speech, which persuaded her soul, compelled the soul it persuaded both to believe what was said and to consent to what was done. So the persuader, as the one who compelled, does wrong; and she who was persuaded, as one compelled by speech, is wrongly blamed.

That persuasion, when it is joined to speech, can stamp the soul in whatever way it wishes, one may learn, first, from the arguments of the astronomers, who, setting one opinion against another, removing one and implanting another, make what is incredible and unseen appear before the eyes of opinion; second, from the compulsory contests fought with speeches, in which a single speech, written with art but not spoken with truth, delights and persuades a great crowd; and third, from the contests of philosophers’ arguments, in which the swiftness of thought is also shown making the belief of opinion easy to change.

The power of speech stands in the same relation to the order of the soul as the ordering of drugs to the nature of bodies. For just as different drugs draw different humours out of the body, and some put an end to illness and others to life, so too with speeches: some cause grief, some delight, some fear, some make their hearers bold, and some drug and bewitch the soul with an evil persuasion.

Now, it has been shown that, if Helen was won over by persuasion, she is deserving of commiseration, and not condemnation. The fourth accusation I shall now proceed to answer with a fourth refutation. For if love was the doer of all these deeds, with no difficulty will she be acquitted of the crime attributed to her. The nature of that which we see is not that which we wish it to be but as it chances to be. For through the vision the soul is also in various ways smitten.

For instance, when hostile bodies put on hostile armour of bronze and iron against the enemy, the one for defence, the other for attack, the sight is at once disturbed and disturbs the soul, so that men often flee in terror from a danger that is still to come. For the truth of the law is driven out by the fear that comes from sight; and when that fear arrives, it makes them disregard both the honour that the law awards and the good that victory brings.

Some people, on seeing frightening things, have lost their presence of mind on the spot: so thoroughly does fear extinguish and drive out thought. And many have fallen into useless labours, terrible diseases and madness hard to cure: so deeply does sight engrave on the mind images of the things it sees. Many frightening things are passed over here, but what is passed over is like what has been said.

Again, when painters complete a single body and figure perfectly out of many colours and bodies, they delight the sight; and the making of statues and the working of images give sweet pleasure to the eyes. So it is natural for sight to grieve at some things and to long for others. Many things work in many people love and longing for many objects and bodies.

If, then, the eye of Helen, charmed by Alexander’s beauty gave to her soul excitement and amorous incitement, what wonder? How could one who was weaker, repel and expel him who, being divine, had power divine? If it was physical diversion and psychical perversion, we should not execrate it as reprehensible but deprecate it as indefensible. For it came to whom it came by fortuitous insinuations not by judicious resolutions; by erotic compulsions, not by despotic machinations.

How, then, is it fair to blame Helen who, whether by love captivated, or by word persuaded, or by violence dominated, or by divine necessity subjugated, did what she did, and is completely absolved from blame?

By this discourse I have freed a woman from evil reputation; I have kept the promise which I made in the beginning; I have essayed to dispose of the injustice of defamation and the folly of allegation; I have prayed to compose a lucubration for Helen’s adulation and my own delectation.

sections.title: Sextus Empiricus, *Against the Logicians* I.65–87
sections.note: Sextus Empiricus's summary of Gorgias's *On What Is Not* (DK 82 B3). Translated for LeetLit from the Greek text of Mutschmann and Mau (Teubner), since no public-domain English version could be found.

text: Gorgias of Leontini belonged to the same company as those who have abolished the criterion, though he did not attack it in the same way as Protagoras and his school. In the work entitled

text.em: On What Is Not, or On Nature

text: he establishes three main points, one after another: first, that nothing is; second, that even if something is, it cannot be grasped by a human being; third, that even if it can be grasped, it certainly cannot be conveyed or explained to anyone else.

That nothing is, he argues as follows. If something is, then either what is is, or what is not, or both what is and what is not. But what is is not, as he will establish; nor is what is not, as he will show; nor both what is and what is not, as he will also teach. Therefore nothing is.

Now what is not is not. For if what is not is, it will at the same time be and not be: insofar as it is thought of as not being, it will not be; but insofar as it is what is not, it will be after all. But it is utterly absurd for something both to be and not to be at the same time; therefore what is not is not. And in another way: if what is not is, what is will not be, for these are opposites of each other; and if being belongs to what is not, not being will belong to what is. But it is not the case that what is is not; so neither will what is not be.

Nor, again, is what is. For if what is is, it is either eternal or generated, or eternal and generated at once. But it is neither eternal nor generated nor both, as we shall show; therefore what is is not. For if what is is eternal (we must begin here), it has no beginning;

for everything that comes to be has a beginning, but the eternal, being ungenerated, had no beginning. Having no beginning, it is unlimited. And if it is unlimited, it is nowhere. For if it is somewhere, that in which it is is something other than it, and so what is, being contained by something, will no longer be unlimited; for the container is greater than the contained, but nothing is greater than the unlimited, so that the unlimited is not anywhere. Nor, again, is it contained in itself;

for then that in which it is and what is in it will be the same, and what is will become two things, place and body (for that in which a thing is is place, and what is in it is body). But this is absurd; so what is is not in itself either. Thus if what is is eternal, it is unlimited; if it is unlimited, it is nowhere; and if it is nowhere, it is not. So if what is is eternal, it is not at all.

Nor, again, can what is be generated. For if it came to be, it came to be either from what is or from what is not. But it did not come to be from what is; for if it is something that is, it did not come to be but already is. Nor from what is not; for what is not cannot generate anything, since whatever generates something must of necessity have a share in existence.

So what is is not generated either. In the same way it is not both together, eternal and generated at once; for these cancel each other: if what is is eternal, it did not come to be, and if it came to be, it is not eternal. So if what is is neither eternal nor generated nor both together, what is would not be.

And in another way: if it is, it is either one or many. But it is neither one nor many, as will be established; therefore what is is not. For if it is one, it is either a quantity, or continuous, or a magnitude, or a body. But whichever of these it is, it is not one: being a quantity, it will be divided; being continuous, it will be cut; similarly, if it is thought of as a magnitude, it will not be indivisible; and if it is a body, it will be threefold, for it will have length, breadth and depth. But it is absurd to say that what is is none of these; so what is is not one.

Nor, again, is it many. For if it is not one, it is not many either; for the many is a combination of ones, so that when the one is abolished, the many are abolished with it. From this, then, it is plain that neither what is is nor what is not is.

That they are not both, what is and what is not, is easy to work out. For if what is not is and what is is, what is not will be the same as what is, as far as being goes; and for this reason neither of them is. For it is agreed that what is not is not; and what is has been shown to be the same as it; so it too will not be.

Moreover, if what is is the same as what is not, they cannot both be; for if they are both, they are not the same, and if they are the same, they are not both. From which it follows that nothing is. For if neither what is is, nor what is not, nor both, and nothing besides these can be conceived, nothing is.

Next it must be shown that even if something is, it is unknowable and unthinkable by a human being. If the things that are thought, says Gorgias, are not things that are, then what is is not thought. And this is reasonable. For just as, if it belonged to the things that are thought to be white, it would also belong to white things to be thought, so, if it belongs to the things that are thought not to be things that are, it will necessarily belong to the things that are not to be thought.

That is why the statement “if the things that are thought are not things that are, what is is not thought” is sound and keeps the sequence. But the things that are thought (for this must be taken first) are not things that are, as we shall establish; therefore what is is not thought. And that the things that are thought are not things that are is plain.

For if the things that are thought are things that are, all the things that are thought are, and in whatever way anyone thinks them. But this is absurd. For if someone thinks of a man flying, or of chariots racing over the sea, a man does not straightaway fly, nor do chariots race over the sea. So the things that are thought are not things that are.

Besides, if the things that are thought are things that are, the things that are not will not be thought. For opposites belong to opposites, and what is not is the opposite of what is; and for this reason, if being thought belongs to what is, not being thought will certainly belong to what is not. But this is absurd; for Scylla and Chimaera and many things that are not are thought. So what is is not thought.

And just as the things that are seen are called visible because they are seen, and the things that are heard are called audible because they are heard, and we do not reject the visible because it is not heard, nor dismiss the audible because it is not seen (for each must be judged by its own sense and not by another), so the things that are thought will also be, even if they are not seen by sight or heard by hearing, because they are grasped by their own criterion.

If, then, someone thinks that chariots are racing over the sea, even if he does not see them, he ought to believe that there are chariots racing over the sea. But this is absurd; so what is is not thought and grasped.

And even if it were grasped, it could not be conveyed to another. For if the things that are are visible and audible and generally perceptible, being things that lie outside us, and of these the visible are grasped by sight and the audible by hearing, and not the other way about, how then can they be made known to another?
For that by which we make things known is speech (

), and speech is not the things that underlie and are. So it is not the things that are that we make known to our neighbours, but speech, which is other than the things that underlie. Just as the visible could not become audible, or the other way about, so, since what is lies outside us, it could not become our speech;

and not being speech, it could not be made clear to another. Speech, he says, is formed from the things that strike us from outside, that is, from perceptible things: from meeting with a flavour, the speech we utter about that quality arises in us, and from the impact of a colour, the speech about the colour. If so, speech does not represent what is outside; rather, what is outside comes to reveal speech.

Nor can one say that speech underlies in the same way as visible and audible things do, so that from it, as something that underlies and is, the things that underlie and are can be made known. For even if speech underlies, he says, it differs from the other things that underlie, and visible bodies differ very greatly from speech; for the visible is grasped by one organ and speech by another. So speech does not display the many things that underlie, just as they do not make plain one another’s nature.

With such difficulties raised by Gorgias, the criterion of truth vanishes, as far as they go; for there could be no criterion of what neither is, nor can be known, nor is by nature able to be shown to another.
